summary: Albania is one of Europe's most open destinations — citizens of the EU, UK, US and dozens more countries enter visa-free for 90 days in any 180 (US passport holders may stay a full year), and most other nationalities can apply online for an e-Visa or enter visa-free with a valid multiple-entry Schengen, UK or US visa.

notes: Flying a drone requires prior authorisation from the Albanian civil aviation authority — do not fly without a permit.

payments.text: Cards are accepted in Tirana hotels, larger restaurants and supermarkets, but Albania remains a cash economy — carry lek for taxis, guesthouses, cafés and anywhere outside the main cities. Euros are often accepted, but at poor rates.

safety.text: Albania is generally safe for travellers, with little violent crime against tourists. The main things to watch are petty theft in crowded areas, assertive local driving and rough road conditions in the mountains.

bestTimeToVisit.text: May, June and September–October bring warm weather without the August crowds on the Riviera; July and August are hottest and busiest.

idp.text: Albania is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognises an International Driving Permit issued under either.

Whether a permit is required in addition to a national licence, and for how long a foreign licence may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Albania yet.

tips.text: Roads to Theth, Valbona and other mountain areas can be rough, narrow and unlit — allow extra time, avoid night driving, and check conditions before renting a car.

If you hold a valid multiple-entry Schengen, UK or US visa (or a residence permit from those countries), you can enter Albania visa-free for up to 90 days even if your passport normally requires a visa.
Pay in lek where you can — prices quoted in euros usually hide a poor exchange rate, and card acceptance drops quickly outside Tirana and the coastal resorts.
US citizens get an unusually generous deal: visa-free entry with permission to stay in Albania for up to one full year.
Summer queues at the land borders with Montenegro and North Macedonia can run to hours around weekends — cross early in the morning if you can.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Albania?
faq.answer: Most travellers do not. Citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia, Japan and dozens of other countries enter visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period (US citizens may stay up to a year). If your passport does need a visa, you can usually apply online at e-visa.al — or enter visa-free if you hold a valid multiple-entry Schengen, UK or US visa.

faq.question: How long can US citizens stay in Albania?
faq.answer: Up to one year visa-free — one of the most generous allowances anywhere in Europe. Stays beyond that require a residence permit from the local authorities.

faq.question: Can I enter Albania with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Yes. A valid multiple-entry Schengen visa (or a Schengen, UK or US residence permit) lets otherwise visa-required nationalities enter Albania visa-free for up to 90 days. Single-entry Schengen visas do not qualify.

faq.question: Is Albania in the Schengen Area or the EU?
faq.answer: No — Albania is an EU candidate country but belongs to neither the EU nor Schengen. Days spent in Albania do not count against your 90/180-day Schengen allowance, which makes it a popular stop for long-term travellers around Europe.

faq.question: What currency is used in Albania, and can I pay in euros?
faq.answer: The Albanian lek (ALL). Euros are widely accepted in tourist areas but usually at an unfavourable rate — withdraw or exchange lek for day-to-day spending, and keep cash on hand outside the main cities.
